question: A 70-year-old man presents with sudden right-sided weakness and dysphasia. Non-contrast CT brain shows a hyperdense lesion in the left basal ganglia. Which type of cerebrovascular accident does this finding represent?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ischaemic stroke does NOT appear as a hyperdense lesion on NCCT; it may show hypodensity or be normal in the acute phase. Hyperdensity indicates fresh blood.
Correct. Fresh blood is hyperdense on non-contrast CT. A hyperdense basal-ganglia lesion in a hypertensive patient is the classic CT signature of intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH).
TIA is defined by resolution of symptoms within 24 hours and does not produce a hyperdense CT lesion. CT is typically normal.
SAH produces hyperdensity in the basal cisterns and sulci, not a focal intra-parenchymal mass. This pattern is ICH.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the Classification of Cerebrovascular Accidents block. The key rule: NCCT must be done before any thrombolysis decision because blood appears hyperdense and must be excluded first.

Well done. The non-contrast CT remains the first-line imaging tool precisely because it reliably distinguishes ischaemic (normal or hypodense) from haemorrhagic (hyperdense) stroke in the acute window.
